title: Scheduled Task/Job: Scheduled Task
summary: This sub-technique is abuse of the Windows Task Scheduler, the richest of the platform schedulers and the one with the most ways to reach it. A task can be registered from the command line with schtasks, through the graphical Task Scheduler console, through a scripting wrapper around the scheduling interfaces, or through remote procedure calls that allow a privileged account on another host to register work without logging on interactively. Each route produces a task definition with triggers, actions and a principal, and the action is what runs when a trigger fires, so the payload is generally a child of the scheduler service rather than of the process that created the task. The evidence set is correspondingly broad: task registration and execution records in the Task Scheduler operational log, the task definition itself on disk and in the registry, and the process creation event for the action, including command line and parent, which is the strongest single artefact. Tasks can also be concealed. If the security descriptor registry value associated with a task is deleted, a step that requires system-level rights, the task can keep running while common enumeration queries no longer show it, and similar tampering with metadata can confuse console views.

beginner.definition: The Windows Task Scheduler is the tool behind the Windows Task Scheduler control panel and the schtasks command. This sub-technique is when an attacker registers their program with it so Windows runs that program later. It is part of the Scheduled Task/Job parent technique. The difference from the other schedulers is that it is the Windows-native one, and it can be driven remotely.
beginner.whyItMatters: Tasks can run as powerful accounts such as SYSTEM, which is the highest local account on Windows. They can start at boot or repeat forever, so the attacker returns after any clean-up. Administrators use tasks for real work every day, which makes malicious ones hard to spot. Some tasks can also be hidden from the usual listing tools.
howItWorks: The attacker decides what should run, such as a script or a file in a temporary folder.
They register a task using schtasks, the console, a scripting wrapper, or a remote call from another machine.
The registration stores the task with its triggers, its action and the account it will run under.
Windows runs the action when a trigger fires, so the new process appears as a child of the scheduler service.
The task can be aimed at a single run, at every logon, or at a repeating interval for lasting access.
Attackers may delete the task's security descriptor so ordinary enumeration no longer reports it.
beginner.example: Think of a hotel front desk that accepts written instructions from guests. A guest writes a note asking staff to open a storage room at two in the morning for a delivery. The desk files the note and follows it exactly, because the request form looks complete. Nothing in the room was broken into, and no alarm sounded. Later, the note is missing from the folder, so the desk cannot explain why the room was opened.
takeaways: The task action and its command line are the most useful evidence to collect.
Tasks can run as SYSTEM, so an alert on a task should be treated as high impact.
Compare the live list of tasks with the definitions stored on disk and in the registry.

objectives: Describe the main ways a Windows scheduled task can be created, including remotely.
Explain how a task action becomes a running process and which account context applies.
Identify the log sources and stored definitions that record task registration and execution.
Explain how a task can be hidden by removing its security descriptor and how to verify the discrepancy.
Distinguish a malicious task from routine administrator and vendor tasks using command line and trigger.
